Senses.Explanation: Sun Bin is the named figure whom these records present as opening or closing a divination shop. Luopu Yuanan announces that 'Sun Bin has closed shop,' calls for another diviner, and then gives a monk a deliberately brutal fortune; Dongshan Fayan reverses the formula by saying Sun Bin opens shop and asks whether anyone born in the ox year wants a reading. Chan records use the recognizable shopkeeper-diviner to stage a public test of who can read whom; the entry does not import a complete biography of the historical strategist.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：奇怪，諸禪德！看此二員作家，一拶一捺，略露風規，大似把手上高山。雖然如是，未免傍觀者哂。且道誰是傍觀者？喝一喝。師到三峰平和尚處，平問：發足甚處？云：黃檗。平云：有何言句？師云：金牛昨夜遭塗炭，直至如今不見蹤。平云：秋風吹玉管，那箇是知音？師云：直透萬重關，不住青霄外。平云：此語太高生。師云：龍生金鳳子，衝破碧琉璃。平云：且坐喫茶。師到襄州華嚴，嚴見來，橫按拄杖作瞌睡勢。師云：莫瞌睡。嚴云：作家禪客，宛爾不同。師云：侍者！點茶來與和尚喫。嚴喚維那：第三位安排著。師到鳳林，林云：有事相借問，得麼？師云：何得剜肉作瘡？林云：海月澄無影，游魚逐浪迷。師云：海月既無影，游魚何得迷？林云：觀風知浪起，翫水野帆飄。師云：孤蟾獨耀江山靜，長嘯一聲天地秋。林云：任將三才輝天地，一句臨機試道看。師云：路逢劒客須呈劒，不是詩人不獻詩。

Senses.Explanation: To draw a snake and add feet is to spoil a sufficient figure by adding what does not belong. Langting Jingting applies the phrase to describing an incomparable mind with an added moon image. Huanglong Huinan uses it for saying more than one's share requires; Shanfeng Xian calls his own further remark an added foot; Juelang Daosheng says the ancestral style never needed such additions. Yuan'an Feng playfully reverses the result—adding feet makes a dragon—while Danxia Dangui tags an old question as the needless addition. The shared Chan test is whether extra speech clarifies the live matter or merely decorates and distorts it.

SearchAliases: a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger
Senses.Explanation: A painted cake is repeatedly named as something that cannot feed: the records apply that bodily limit to words, talk, blows, and shouts that likewise fail to satisfy hunger. Literally a cake drawn or painted rather than edible. Chan records make it a stock verdict by completing the image: “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” . In the Xiangyan case, after he cannot answer Guishan's question and searches all the writings he has read for a reply, he sighs, “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” ; the record then has him burn those writings. Dahui's verse pairs it with another ineffective likeness: “how could a shimmering mirage ever stop thirst? When could a painted cake fill hunger?” . The verdict extends beyond writings. One discourse says “discussing the obscure and speaking of the marvelous is like using a painted cake to fill hunger” ; another asks whether wielding the staff and shouting differs from filling hunger with a painted cake . A verse explicitly places it beside “speaking of food never makes one full” . Thus the object keeps its literal non-feeding property while the corpus repeatedly applies it to quoted words, explanations, stock gestures, and other substitutes that it says do not fill hunger.

Senses.Explanation: A donkey-tethering stake is a post to which a donkey is fastened. Chan speakers call bodhi and nirvana, teaching collections, and fixed formulations donkey-tethering stakes. Boatman Decheng makes the verbal deployment explicit: “one phrase that fits the head—ten thousand aeons a donkey-tethering stake.” The stake remains the concrete tethering object; Zen bends it into a name for words or teachings at which someone stays tied.
